To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
older women's cancer experiences are not necessarily continuous with their life trajectories, but are rather shaped by the interplay between the social and the individual.

(1) older women's cancer stories are not always characterized by a lack of disruption; (2) older women's narratives are shaped by cultural, moral, interactional and structural factors that foreclose disruption; (3) these foreclosures are not always experienced as positive or liberating.

older women's narratives suggest that the experience of cancer may or may not be biographically disruptive and, when cancer is assessed as non-disrupting, it is not because the women have a `continuous' or'reinforcing' life, but rather because they are constrained from narrating their lives as biographically disrupted.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the extent to which the experience of chronic disease is socially constructed and how this may vary across the lifecourse.

the ways in which the experience of chronic disease is shaped by the interplay between individual and social factors, and how the social study of illness can be enriched by a more nuanced understanding of the relationship between biography and chronic illness.
the social construction of older women's experiences of chronic illness and with the social and cultural processes that constrain or enable the telling of those experiences.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
chronic illness is biographically disruptive for some older women, and non-disruptive for others, and that the assessment of illness as disruptive or not is shaped by a range of factors.
disruption is a matter of perspective and that the experience of cancer is not always disruptive, nor does it always disrupt lives.
the experience of cancer is not necessarily disruptive for older women.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
older women are not necessarily more accepting of cancer than their younger counterparts, but that they are more constrained in the way they talk about it.

the disruption foreclosed by older women with cancer is not the disruption of the biographical narrative per se, but of a disruption of the biographically continuous and the biographically reinforcing.

the study offers a challenge to the notion that the experience of chronic disease in old age is inherently non-disruptive and that the study offers an account of the social conditions that render disruption difficult to articulate.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the experience of chronic health conditions is not a simple reflection of the social and cultural context in which people live.
, in the case of older women with cancer, the experience of disruption may be foreclosed, rather than continuous.
, while the idea of chronic illness as `biographical disruption' has been usefully challenged, it has not been adequately replaced.
